description: Advertising mediums, sales promotion techniques and PR methods for small businesses.
content_html:
Promotion in the Marketing Mix

Promotion is the fourth P in the marketing mix. It covers everything a business does to raise awareness of its products and encourage purchase. A common misconception is that promotion and advertising are the same thing. They are not: advertising is just one type of promotion. Promotion also includes sales promotion techniques and public relations. This lesson covers all three.

Advertising Mediums

An advertising medium is the channel through which an advert reaches its audience. Start-ups must choose mediums that match their budget, their target audience and their brand image. Advertising mediums split into two broad groups: traditional (non-digital) and digital.

Non-digital advertising mediums include:

  • Leaflets — low-cost printed flyers, posted through letterboxes or handed out at events. Useful for local businesses targeting a specific area.
  • Newspapers — local or national print advertising. A local fish-and-chip shop might advertise in the town’s weekly paper to reach nearby residents.
  • Magazines — specialist publications allow the business to reach a defined interest group. A small outdoor clothing brand might advertise in a hiking magazine to find customers who already love walking.
  • Radio — adverts on local radio stations reach a broad local audience during commuting hours.
  • Billboards — large outdoor displays in high-footfall areas such as roadsides or shopping centres, suitable for building brand awareness over time.
  • Cinema — adverts shown before films reach a captive audience and can be targeted by film genre and local cinema location.
  • TV adverts — television advertising gives a business wide reach and strong visual impact. It is traditionally expensive, but regional TV slots can be more accessible for a small business. TV adverts are a named medium in the specification, added to the list in 2025.
Key Fact

The seven non-digital advertising mediums are: leaflets, newspapers, magazines, radio, billboards, cinema and TV adverts. TV adverts are the most recent addition to the list. A start-up on a tight budget will typically start with leaflets or local newspapers, while TV advertising requires a significantly larger spend.

Digital Advertising Mediums

Digital channels allow start-ups to reach specific audiences at lower cost than most traditional mediums. The named digital advertising mediums are:

  • Social media — platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Facebook allow businesses to post content, run paid adverts and communicate directly with followers. There are two distinct types of social media post, and the specification requires you to know the difference:
    • Business-generated posts — content created and controlled by the business itself (a photo of a new product, an announcement of opening hours, a promotional offer).
    • Third-party-generated posts — content created by customers, bloggers or influencers about the business or its products. The business does not control these, but positive third-party posts can be highly persuasive because they are seen as independent opinions rather than paid advertising.
  • Social networks — broader networking platforms where businesses can create communities, run groups or participate in conversations relevant to their audience.
  • Websites — a business’s own website is a digital shopfront. Good search-engine visibility drives customers to it without the ongoing cost of paid adverts.
  • Online banners — paid display adverts that appear on websites, targeted to users based on their browsing interests.
  • SMS (text messages) — promotional texts sent directly to customers who have opted in, delivering offers or updates instantly.
  • Podcasts — a business can sponsor an existing podcast relevant to its target audience, or create its own branded podcast to build an engaged listener community.
  • Vlogs (video blogs) — video content, typically on platforms such as YouTube, allows a business or individual to demonstrate products, share behind-the-scenes content or build a following over time.

This distinction matters in the exam. A business-generated post is planned, written and published by the business — it is under the business’s control, can be timed and targeted, but customers may view it sceptically because it is obviously self-promotional. A third-party-generated post comes from a customer review, a blogger’s write-up or an influencer’s recommendation — the business does not control what is said, but positive third-party posts tend to be more trusted because they appear independent. A start-up encouraging customers to leave reviews or tag them on social media is leveraging third-party generation.

Sales Promotion Techniques

Sales promotion techniques are time-limited tactics used to stimulate sales quickly. Unlike advertising, which builds awareness over time, sales promotion is designed to get customers to buy now. The seven techniques you need to know are:

  • Discounts — reducing the price for a limited time (for example, “20% off this weekend only”). Effective for clearing stock or attracting price-sensitive customers.
  • Competitions — customers enter a prize draw when they buy. Creates excitement and encourages purchase without permanently reducing the price.
  • BOGOF (Buy One Get One Free) — a form of discount where two units are sold for the price of one, doubling the perceived value.
  • Point of sale displays — eye-catching promotional material at the checkout or near the product in a physical location, encouraging impulse buying.
  • Free gifts — a free item given with a purchase (for example, a free tote bag with a first order). Adds perceived value without reducing the main product’s price.
  • Loyalty schemes — customers earn points or stamps with each purchase that can be exchanged for discounts or free products, encouraging repeat business.
  • Sponsorship — a business provides financial or in-kind support to an event, organisation or individual in exchange for brand visibility. A local bakery sponsoring a community fun run gets its name on race bibs and banners.
Key Fact

The seven sales promotion techniques are: discounts, competitions, BOGOF, point of sale, free gifts, loyalty schemes and sponsorship. Short-term promotions can drive immediate sales, but using discounts too frequently may train customers to wait for a deal rather than paying full price — a risk for a start-up trying to build a premium image.

Public Relations for Small Businesses

Public relations (PR) is about building and maintaining a positive reputation through unpaid coverage. Unlike advertising, PR is not directly paid for — a business earns media attention by doing or creating something genuinely interesting or newsworthy. For a small start-up, PR can be a cost-effective way to reach audiences that paid advertising could not afford. The three PR methods you need to know are:

  • Product placement — getting the product into a TV show, film, video or prominent social media post without it being explicitly labelled as an advert. A small candle-maker whose candles appear in a popular lifestyle blogger’s video benefits from organic exposure.
  • Celebrity endorsement — a well-known individual publicly recommends or uses the product. For a start-up, this might mean a local sports personality or community figure using and sharing the product on their social channels rather than a national celebrity deal.
  • Press releases — a written statement sent to journalists, local newspapers, bloggers or radio stations announcing something newsworthy about the business — a launch, a charity partnership, a milestone or an award. If picked up by the media, it generates free coverage.

Advertising is guaranteed to appear — the business pays and the advert runs. PR coverage is not guaranteed: a press release may be ignored, a celebrity endorsement may receive backlash, or a product placement may go unnoticed. However, when PR works, it tends to be more credible than advertising because it appears to come from a neutral source (a journalist, a blogger, a local figure) rather than from the business itself. For a small start-up on a limited budget, a well-timed press release about a local award or community project can generate the same reach as a paid advert at zero cost.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on advertising questions is treating “promotion” and “advertising” as the same thing — advertising is one type of promotion, not the whole category. Make sure you know and can distinguish all seven non-digital mediums including TV adverts (added in 2025, which means early exam series are likely to test this specifically). For social media questions, always clarify whether you are describing a business-generated post (controlled by the business) or a third-party-generated post (created by customers or influencers) — the specification treats these as separate and an examiner will expect the distinction. On 6-mark “Analyse” questions about promotional choices, embed the scenario business name and a specific detail (budget, product, target audience) in your first sentence, then build your analytical chains from there. Generic answers that apply equally to any business will stall below the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Advertising mediums include seven non-digital types (leaflets, newspapers, magazines, radio, billboards, cinema, TV adverts) and seven digital types (social media, social networks, websites, online banners, SMS, podcasts, vlogs). Social media posts split into business-generated (controlled by the business) and third-party-generated (by customers or influencers).
  • The seven sales promotion techniques are discounts, competitions, BOGOF, point of sale, free gifts, loyalty schemes and sponsorship. These are short-term tactics designed to drive an immediate purchase decision.
  • Public relations (PR) builds a positive reputation through unpaid media coverage. The three PR methods are product placement, celebrity endorsement and press releases. PR is generally lower cost than advertising but less predictable — coverage is earned, not guaranteed.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a third-party-generated social media post?
A) A business posting a photo of its new product on its own Instagram account
B) A business sending an SMS discount code to its mailing list
C) A customer sharing a positive review of a product on their personal blog
D) A business publishing a press release on its own website
practice_questions.marks: C) A customer sharing a positive review of a product on their personal blog [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage of using a press release as a PR method for a small start-up.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: it generates media coverage at no direct cost to the business; it is perceived as more credible than paid advertising because it comes from a neutral media source; it can reach a wide audience if picked up by local newspapers, radio or online publications. [1 mark for any one relevant advantage stated clearly.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two digital advertising mediums that a start-up selling eco-friendly stationery might use to reach customers.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following, each with enough description to show understanding:
• Social media (business-generated posts) — posting images of the product on platforms such as Instagram, with content reflecting the eco-friendly values of the brand to attract environmentally conscious customers. [1 mark]
• Podcasts (sponsorship) — sponsoring a podcast focused on sustainable living to reach listeners who already care about eco-friendly choices. [1 mark]
• Vlogs — creating video content demonstrating how the stationery is made from recycled materials, published on YouTube, to build brand authenticity and reach. [1 mark]
• Online banners — targeted display adverts shown to users who have searched for eco-friendly products. [1 mark]
[2 marks for any two named digital mediums with relevant description applied to the stationery context.]

practice_questions.text:
Yarrow & Stem is a small Ltd company in Hereford run by two founders, selling wildflower seed packets. They want to boost sales quickly before the spring planting season and have a promotional budget of £400. They are considering either a BOGOF offer or a local radio advertising campaign.

Justify which promotional option you would recommend to Yarrow & Stem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and developed with specific reference to the scenario (seasonal urgency, £400 budget, wildflower seed packets, small Ltd). The recommended option's advantages are explained with good reason chains, and at least one drawback of the recommended option or advantage of the alternative is acknowledged. The justification is grounded in the specific context — for example, BOGOF directly incentivises immediate purchase (important before spring), costs no cash outlay beyond reduced margin, and is easy to implement on a £400 budget; alternatively, radio can reach a local audience quickly and generate awareness beyond existing customers, but £400 may be insufficient for a campaign with meaningful reach. A developed conclusion adds a new evaluative point — for example, that BOGOF is the better choice because Yarrow & Stem needs to sell existing stock quickly rather than build long-term awareness.

Secure (3–4 marks): A clear recommendation with developed reasoning that uses some scenario detail. At least one reason chain is clear. Some acknowledgement of trade-offs.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with basic reasoning. Limited engagement with the specific scenario.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with little or no supporting reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Greybridge Brew Co is a small partnership in Sheffield producing craft coffee. The founders, Marcus and Amara, are deciding between two promotional approaches:

Option A: Invest £600 in a TV advert on a regional channel to reach a broad local audience.
Option B: Invite a popular local food blogger with 18,000 followers to try the coffee and write a review.

Analyse how each option might help Greybridge Brew Co achieve its promotional objectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Analyses both options with clear analytical chains and specific reference to the scenario. For Option A (TV advert): strong visual impact and broad reach, but expensive for a small partnership (£600 may buy limited airtime on regional TV); the advert is controlled by the business but is obviously promotional, which may not build the same trust as editorial coverage. For Option B (blogger review): a third-party-generated post that is perceived as independent and trustworthy by the blogger's 18,000 followers; it may cost nothing or a very small fee (product sample), meaning more of the promotional budget is preserved; however, the business cannot control what the blogger writes and a neutral or negative review could damage reputation. Explores the trade-offs explicitly and reaches a supported analytical conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one advantage of each option with some analytical development. Some reference to the scenario.

Developing (2 marks): Describes the two options without clear analytical chains or scenario engagement.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one or both options with minimal analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Bluebell Bath Co is a sole trader in Norwich making luxury bath products. The owner, Faye, wants to build a loyal customer base and is considering introducing a loyalty scheme.

Discuss whether a loyalty scheme is likely to be the most effective sales promotion technique for Bluebell Bath Co.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Develops both sides of the argument with clear reasoning and specific application to the scenario (luxury bath products, sole trader, building a loyal customer base). In favour: a loyalty scheme rewards repeat purchase directly, which aligns with Faye's objective of building a loyal base; it encourages customers to return rather than switching to a competitor for a lower-priced alternative; for a small business, knowing customers will return provides a more stable revenue base. Against: a loyalty scheme alone does not attract new customers — if awareness is low, there is nobody to retain; the administrative cost of running a points or stamp scheme may be significant for a sole trader with no support staff; other techniques such as a BOGOF on a bestselling product or a competition on social media might generate more immediate buzz and new customer acquisition. Evaluative conclusion adds new thinking — for example, that loyalty schemes work best once a customer base already exists, so Faye should focus first on advertising or PR to attract new customers, then introduce a loyalty scheme to retain them.

Secure (5–7 marks): Addresses both sides with some development and scenario reference. Conclusion is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies advantages or disadvantages of a loyalty scheme with limited balance or scenario application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): States a view with little justification or scenario engagement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a business-generated social media post?
options: A customer tagging the business in a review on their personal account
A blogger writing about the product without being asked
The business posting a new product photo on its own Instagram page
A journalist mentioning the product in a newspaper article

knowledge_checks.q: Which advertising medium was added to the specification in 2025?
A buy-one-get-one-free deal is an example of a sales promotion technique known as _____.
A press release, celebrity endorsement and product placement are all examples of _____ (PR) methods.
Match each promotional method to its description:
right: A written statement sent to media announcing something newsworthy
Customers earn points or stamps redeemable for rewards
Getting a product featured in a video or programme without it being labelled as an advert

flashcard_questions.q: Is advertising the same as promotion?
flashcard_questions.a: No — advertising is one type of promotion; promotion also includes sales promotion and PR.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the seven non-digital advertising mediums.
flashcard_questions.a: Leaflets, newspapers, magazines, radio, billboards, cinema, TV adverts.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a business-generated social media post?
flashcard_questions.a: Content created and published by the business itself on its own social media account.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a third-party-generated social media post?
flashcard_questions.a: Content about the business created by customers, bloggers or influencers — not controlled by the business.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of social media post tends to be more trusted by customers — business-generated or third-party-generated?
flashcard_questions.a: Third-party-generated — it appears independent rather than self-promotional.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the seven sales promotion techniques.
flashcard_questions.a: Discounts, competitions, BOGOF, point of sale, free gifts, loyalty schemes, sponsorship.
Activities that manage public perception through unpaid media coverage and community relationships.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three PR methods on the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Product placement, celebrity endorsement and press releases.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a press release be more cost-effective than advertising for a start-up?
flashcard_questions.a: It generates media coverage at no direct cost if picked up by journalists or bloggers.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one risk of relying on PR instead of advertising.
flashcard_questions.a: Coverage is not guaranteed — a press release can be ignored or a review can be negative.
A system where customers earn points or stamps per purchase, redeemable for discounts or free items.

glossary_terms.definition: All the activities a business uses to communicate its product to potential customers and persuade them to buy.
Paid communications in specific media designed to reach a wide audience and build brand awareness or drive sales.
Short-term incentives designed to encourage an immediate purchase decision from customers.
Activities that manage how a business is perceived by the public, using unpaid media coverage and community relationships rather than paid advertising.
Content created and published by the business itself on its own social media accounts, under the business's direct control.
Content about a business or its products created by customers, bloggers or influencers rather than the business itself.
